articles.title: Satellite imagery is already free. Detail is the expensive part.
articles.author: EarthViewer
articles.summary: Sentinel-2 covers the whole planet every few days and costs nothing. What it cannot do is resolve a courtyard — and that gap is the one applied-view exists to close.
articles.body:
Every few days, two satellites photograph the entire land surface of the Earth and give the results away. Sentinel-2 has been doing it since 2015. Sentinel-1 does the same with radar, which does not care about cloud, smoke or darkness. Nobody charges for either one. There is no account, no key, no licence negotiated per scene.

So when people say satellite imagery is expensive, they do not quite mean imagery. They mean detail.

## Where the money actually goes

Sentinel-2's sharpest bands sample the ground every ten metres. One pixel covers a tennis court.

That is enough — genuinely enough — for a great deal. A flood. A burn scar. A new quarry. A field turning through a season. A coastline moving over five years. If your question lives at that scale, the free data answers it, and the numbers underneath the picture will hold up in an argument.

It is not enough to see a car, a roof panel, or the trees along a street. For that you need a metre or better, and that is where the price sits. Commercial operators charge by the scene, licence what you may do with the result, and often will not sell you the archive at all.

The outcome is a strange gap. Anyone can look at the whole planet for nothing, and almost nobody can look at their own street.

## Closing the gap honestly

EarthViewer's answer is a thing we call applied-view, and it is worth explaining exactly, because the temptation here is to overclaim.

Existing high-detail imagery of a place is registered onto a fresh Sentinel pass. The new pass carries what is true now — colour, change, radar, heat, cloud. The existing layer carries the fine texture that ten-metre pixels never held. What comes out looks like the place, at a definition free data alone cannot reach.

It is built from two sources rather than measured from one. That is the whole trick, and there is no cleverness hiding in it: no upscaling model, no diffusion, nothing inventing a plausible street. Every pixel came from either a satellite measurement or an existing photograph of that same ground.

Underneath the picture the measurements stay in their own units. Click anywhere and you get reflectance, or backscatter in decibels, or NDVI — the actual numbers, not an impression of them.

## What it will not do

Three things, said plainly.

It cannot date the fine detail. The texture came from the existing layer, recorded at some other time. If you need to know how a place looked on a particular day, that is the fresh pass only, and the fresh pass is ten metres.

It cannot evidence an event. Damage, movement, anything at the scale of a vehicle or a roof: applied-view will render it convincingly and cannot prove it. For that you need the original high-resolution source.

It runs out. Zoom far enough past what the existing layer holds and it smears, the same as anything else. There is a pair of frames of Heathrow on the front page showing exactly that, because a limit you can see is worth more than one you find out about later.

## Why give it away

Because the data underneath already is. Copernicus and NASA publish theirs openly and it is genuinely good — the constraint is resolution, not quality. Building a paywall on top of free public data to sell a view of it would be a strange thing to do.

So: one Python file. It installs what it needs on first run and opens in its own window. No sign-up, no API key, no token, no trial.

Look at your own street. Then look at a fire front in Australia, a flood in Pakistan, the ice going out of a Norwegian fjord — all from the same window, on the same afternoon, for nothing.

That is the part worth being pleased about. Not that the imagery is cheap. That it was always there, and now it is easier to look at.
